sections.html:
Paducah sits where the Tennessee River meets the Ohio River, roughly halfway between St. Louis and Nashville, and McCracken County runs its government from here. No other Jackson Purchase city is bigger, and the metro area held 103,481 people in 2020. The city covers about 20 square miles of land.

Steamboat repair yards and the Illinois Central shops, completed in 1927, built the older neighborhoods that many sellers now own. A house here is often tied to river history, which shows up in how buyers look at flood maps and old brick.

The July 2025 estimate is 26,730 people living in 11,741 households of about 2.19 people each. Homeowners hold 55.0 percent of those households, which leaves a lot of rental stock in town.

  • Typical home value, 2020 through 2024 data: $165,300.
  • Monthly cost of owning: $1,323 with a mortgage and $519 without.
  • Typical rent: $834.
  • Median household income: $49,915.

With values in that range, a roof or foundation bill can eat a big slice of the equity. Sellers in that spot often prefer a buyer who needs no lender inspection.

The river's biggest test came in 1937. The Ohio crested at 60.8 feet on February 2, well past the 50 foot flood stage, and about 27,000 residents left their homes for nearly three weeks. Congress then directed the Corps of Engineers to build the floodwall that guards downtown.

Paducah joined FEMA's flood insurance program and, under Chapter 50 of its code, controls building inside Special Flood Hazard Areas. Sixteen flood map panels cover the city. Anyone developing in a hazard area needs a permit application with a $100 fee, plans from a Kentucky registered engineer or architect, and a FEMA Elevation Certificate. Insurers use that same certificate to price a policy, so a buyer's insurance agent may ask for it. Call the Engineering Department at 270-444-8511 to learn whether an address sits in a mapped zone.

Lower Town is the oldest neighborhood. Most of its buildings went up after the Civil War, and the Artist Relocation Program has offered incentives for artists to buy and restore homes there since August 2000. A twenty block stretch of downtown is a listed historic district.

  • In the H-1 and H-2 historic zones, exterior changes that show from the street need a Certificate of Appropriateness.
  • Tearing down a structure inside the Demolition Control Zone needs a demolition control permit, with the Planning Director, Chief Building Inspector and a historic commission chair signing off.
  • New or heavily renovated buildings need a final inspection before anyone moves in.
  • The Building Division at 270-444-8690 can confirm whether liens or fines are attached to a property address.

Make that call before choosing an asking price, because an open fine or unpermitted work can slow a closing.

Paducah Public Schools serves part of the city, and other addresses belong to McCracken County Public Schools. Check which district a house is zoned for before you advertise it. Interstate 24 runs east to Nashville and west toward St. Louis, with a business loop through downtown, and Interstate 69 curves around the east side.

Summers are hot and damp, with roughly 50 inches of annual precipitation and the odd tornado outbreak. Expect buyers to ask about roof age and drainage.

Kentucky fixes real estate values on January 1 each year, and the county's Property Valuation Administrator sets them. That office neither sets rates nor takes payment. Bills become payable at the Sheriff's office on November 1, and paying in full on or before that date trims 2 percent. From November 2 to December 31 the face amount is due. A January payment carries a 5 percent penalty, and anything paid after January 31 carries 10 percent (KRS 134.015).

The Sheriff keeps open bills until April 15. They then pass to the County Clerk, where interest and penalty build at 1 percent a month, a lien goes on record, and a private investor may buy the bill at a yearly sale normally held in October. The County Attorney's office offers installment plans, and a bill on a current plan is marked unavailable for sale. A lien on file can stall a closing until the balance is cleared.

Each year the roll opens for public review in early May and stays open 13 days (KRS 133.045). Start by asking the PVA for a conference, and bring recent neighborhood sales, an appraisal under two years old, or photos and a repair list for a condition appeal. If the conference fails, file with the Clerk, and a three person local panel rules. Anyone still unhappy can go on to the state's Board of Tax Appeals.

Owners 65 and over, or totally disabled, can apply to the PVA for the homestead or disability exemption.

sections.h2: Closing costs and who to call
sections.html:
Kentucky puts its deed transfer tax on the seller: $0.50 for each $500 of price or part of one, collected at the recording counter (KRS 142.050). Foreclosure deeds, divorce transfers between spouses and nominal parent to child deeds are exempt.

Paducah offices to call before listing
OfficeHandlesPhone
Engineering DepartmentFlood hazard maps and elevation certificates270-444-8511
Community Development, Building DivisionPermits, zoning, liens and fines on an address270-444-8690
McCracken County PVAAssessments, exemptions, appeals270-444-4712

Hiring an agent puts the house in front of the most buyers, though repairs, showings and a lender's timeline come with it. Selling on your own saves the commission and hands you the marketing and paperwork. A cash offer from an investor skips repairs and appraisals, which can suit a house with flood history, a tired roof or an open code case. Add up what you would keep from each route after transfer tax, tax proration and any lien payoff.

Whichever you pick, request a payoff amount from the Sheriff or Clerk and your lender before you accept terms, and check the Building Division for liens or fines on the address. At closing the title search turns up any open item, you sign the deed, and the transfer tax is paid when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Is Paducah in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Some of it is. The city maps Special Flood Hazard Areas on 16 FEMA map panels, and the Engineering Department at 270-444-8511 can tell you whether a specific address falls inside one. A mapped address can mean a buyer needs flood insurance, and an elevation certificate helps price that policy.

faqs.q: Which office collects Paducah's property tax bill?
faqs.a: Current bills are paid to the McCracken County Sheriff from November 1. The County Clerk takes over bills still open after April 15. Values come from the PVA, which handles no payments.

faqs.q: What if I still owe taxes when I sell?
faqs.a: Open taxes become a lien at the County Clerk, and the closing agent normally pays that lien from your sale proceeds. The late charge steps up twice after year end, and the Clerk adds 1 percent a month once it holds the bill. Request a payoff amount from the Sheriff or Clerk ahead of closing day.

faqs.q: Does tearing down an old building in Paducah take a permit?
faqs.a: Maybe. Inside the Demolition Control Zone you need a demolition control permit approved by city staff and a historic commission chair, and you bring redevelopment plans. Call Community Development at 270-444-8690 to check the zone for your address.

faqs.q: What does Kentucky's deed tax come to on a Paducah sale?
faqs.a: Fifty cents for each $500 of price. The clerk takes it when the deed goes on record, and KRS 142.050 exempts foreclosure deeds and certain family transfers.
